title: Design a Photo-Sharing Service
summary: An Instagram-style service where users upload photos, follow others, and browse a media-rich feed. The signature challenge is separating heavy binary media (blob storage + CDN) from lightweight metadata (a DB), processing uploads asynchronously into multiple sizes, and generating a feed over a media-heavy read-dominated workload.
keyTakeaways: Store the photo bytes in blob storage (S3) and serve them via CDN; keep only metadata + the media URL in the DB — never blobs in the DB.
Upload is a two-phase flow: write the original to blob storage, then enqueue async resize/thumbnail/transcode work.
A queue-driven media pipeline generates multiple sizes (thumbnail, feed, full) so clients fetch the right resolution.
Metadata (photoId, ownerId, caption, mediaUrls, ts) lives in a sharded DB keyed by photo or user.
Feed generation reuses fan-out (push/pull hybrid), but the feed carries media URLs, not bytes — hydration is a CDN fetch.
The workload is overwhelmingly read-heavy and bandwidth-dominated; CDN hit rate is the primary scaling lever.
Decoupling media from metadata lets each scale independently — blob storage for capacity, DB for query, CDN for delivery.

functional: Upload photos with captions; follow users; media-rich home feed and profile grid; likes/comments optional.
Durability of media is paramount — a user's photos are irreplaceable.
scale: 100M DAU · 10M uploads/day · ~2 MB stored per photo across all variants · 100:1 view:upload
20 TB/day of new media → ~7.3 PB/yr, ~22 PB at 3× replication
~200 TB/day egress → must be CDN-served, not origin. Metadata (~1 KB/photo) is a rounding error.

questions.prompt: Open the design: functional and non-functional requirements for a photo-sharing service, and what makes it different from a text feed.
points: Functional: upload photos (with caption); follow users; view a media feed; view a user's profile grid; like/comment (optional).
Non-functional: highly read-heavy, bandwidth-dominated (media is MBs, not KBs), low feed/media latency, high durability (never lose a user's photos).
Durability of media is paramount — photos are irreplaceable, so replicated blob storage.
The differentiator vs a text feed: large binary payloads, so storage/delivery of bytes dominates over the metadata/feed logic.
Confirm scale: DAU, uploads/day, avg photo size, read:write ratio, follower distribution.
questions.answer: Functionally: upload photos with captions, follow users, browse a media-rich home feed and profile grids, and optionally like/comment. Non-functionally it's extremely read-heavy and bandwidth-dominated — payloads are megabytes, not kilobytes — so I optimize media delivery latency and, critically, durability, because a user's photos are irreplaceable. What sets it apart from a text feed is exactly that binary weight: the hard part shifts from feed logic to storing and delivering bytes cheaply and durably. I'd confirm DAU, uploads/day, average photo size, and the follower distribution up front.

questions.prompt: Estimate capacity. Assume 100M DAU, 10M photo uploads/day, average stored size 2MB (across all generated variants), and a 100:1 read:view ratio. Derive upload QPS, new storage/day and /year, and read bandwidth.
points: Uploads: 10M/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 116 uploads/s; peak ~2–3× ≈ 300/s.
New media storage: 10M × 2MB = 20 TB/day → ~7.3 PB/year (before replication; ~22 PB at 3× replication).
Views: 100:1 → 1B photo-views/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ ~11.6K reads/s; peak ≈ 23K+/s.
Read bandwidth: at ~200KB per delivered (feed-size) image, 1B views/day ≈ 200 TB/day egress — served from CDN, not origin.
Metadata is tiny by comparison (~1KB/photo) — the cost and scale story is entirely media bytes + egress.
questions.answer: 10M uploads/day is only ~116/s, ~300/s at peak — writes are modest. But at 2MB stored per photo across variants that's 20 TB/day of new media, ~7.3 PB/year before replication and roughly 22 PB at 3× durability. On the read side, 100:1 gives 1B photo-views/day, ~12K reads/s, and at ~200KB per delivered feed image that's on the order of 200 TB/day of egress — which is why this must be served from CDN, not origin. Metadata is a rounding error at ~1KB/photo; the entire cost and scale story is media bytes and bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Design the upload and read APIs. How does a client upload a large photo, and how does it fetch feed media?
points: Upload: request a pre-signed/direct upload URL, PUT the bytes straight to blob storage (bypassing the app tier), then POST /photos {mediaKey, caption} to register metadata.
Alternatively POST /photos multipart → app streams to blob store (simpler but app-tier bandwidth cost).
Register returns photoId; processing status is async.
Read: GET /feed?cursor=&limit → returns metadata + CDN media URLs per size; client picks resolution.
GET /users/{id}/photos for the profile grid (thumbnails).
questions.answer: For upload I prefer a direct-to-blob flow: the client asks for a pre-signed URL, PUTs the bytes straight to S3 (bypassing the app tier so we don't pay app bandwidth), then calls `POST /photos {mediaKey, caption}` to register metadata and returns a photoId, with processing done async. Reads are metadata-plus-URLs: `GET /feed?cursor=&limit` returns each post's metadata and a set of CDN URLs (thumbnail/feed/full) so the client fetches the right resolution directly from the CDN, and `GET /users/{id}/photos` backs the thumbnail profile grid.

questions.prompt: Give the high-level architecture and the data model, emphasizing the media/metadata split.
points: Components: app tier, blob storage (S3) for originals + variants, CDN for delivery, metadata DB (sharded), a queue + worker pool for processing, feed service.
Media path is fully separate from metadata: blobs in S3, URLs/metadata in the DB.
Data model: Photos{photoId, ownerId, caption, mediaKeys{thumb,feed,full}, createdAt, status}; Follows{followerId, followeeId}; Feed{userId → [photoId...]}.
Feed rows carry photoIds → hydrate to metadata → resolve to CDN URLs; bytes never touch the DB or feed store.
Each layer scales independently: S3 for capacity/durability, DB for queries, CDN for egress, workers for processing throughput.
questions.answer: The key move is separating media from metadata. Photo bytes — original and generated variants — live in blob storage (S3) and are delivered by CDN; the DB holds only metadata and the media keys/URLs. Components are an app tier, S3, CDN, a sharded metadata DB, and a queue with a worker pool for processing, plus a feed service. The model is `Photos{photoId, ownerId, caption, mediaKeys{thumb,feed,full}, createdAt, status}`, `Follows`, and per-user `Feed{userId → [photoId…]}`. Feed rows carry photo IDs that hydrate to metadata and resolve to CDN URLs — bytes never touch the DB or the feed store — so blob storage, the DB, the CDN, and the worker pool each scale on their own axis.

questions.q: Where should the actual photo bytes be stored, and how served?
options: As BLOB columns in the relational metadata DB, served through the app tier
In distributed blob/object storage (e.g. S3) with only the URL/key in the DB, served via CDN
In Redis alongside the feed post IDs for fast access
On the app servers' local disks, load-balanced across them
questions.explain: Photos are large, immutable binaries — object storage (S3) is built for exactly this: cheap, effectively unbounded, replicated for durability. The DB stores just the key/URL and metadata so it stays small and queryable, and delivery goes through a CDN to serve the bandwidth close to users. BLOBs in the DB bloat it and kill query performance; Redis is expensive RAM for MB payloads; and local app-server disks aren't durable or shareable.

questions.prompt: Crux deep dive: design the asynchronous media-processing pipeline. Why async, what runs, and what does the client see before processing finishes?
points: Why async: resizing/transcoding a 2MB+ image takes seconds — doing it inline blocks the upload and couples user latency to CPU work.
Flow: original lands in S3 → an event/message goes on a queue → a worker pool pulls jobs and generates thumbnail/feed/full variants (+ format transcode, EXIF strip, moderation).
Workers write variants back to S3 and update the photo's status/mediaKeys in the DB.
Client sees status=processing (show original or a placeholder), flips to ready when variants exist — or upload is confirmed immediately and variants appear shortly after.
Queue gives elasticity + retry + backpressure: spikes buffer, failed jobs retry, workers scale independently.
Idempotent workers (keyed on photoId+variant) so retries don't duplicate work.
questions.answer: Resizing and transcoding a multi-megabyte image takes seconds of CPU, so doing it inline would block the upload and tie user latency to that work — hence async. The original lands in S3, which emits an event onto a queue; a worker pool pulls jobs and produces the variants (thumbnail, feed, full), transcodes format, strips EXIF, and runs moderation, then writes them back to S3 and updates the photo's `status` and `mediaKeys` in the DB. The client gets an immediate upload confirmation with `status=processing` — showing the original or a placeholder — and flips to ready once variants exist. The queue is what makes this robust: it buffers upload spikes, retries failed jobs, applies backpressure, and lets processing workers scale independently, with jobs keyed by photoId+variant so retries stay idempotent.

questions.q: The service is overwhelmingly read-heavy and bandwidth-dominated. What is the single most important lever for scaling media delivery?
options: Adding read replicas to the metadata database
Sharding the feed store across more Redis nodes
Maximizing CDN cache hit rate so most image bytes are served from edge caches, not origin/S3
Vertically scaling the app tier with more CPU
questions.explain: The dominant cost and latency is delivering hundreds of TB/day of image bytes, and photo access is power-law skewed toward recent/popular content — so a high CDN cache hit rate means the vast majority of bytes are served from edge caches near users, sparing origin/S3 bandwidth and slashing latency. Metadata replicas, feed-store shards, and app CPU all matter, but they address the tiny metadata/logic side, not the bytes that actually saturate the system.

questions.prompt: Explain feed generation here. How do you reuse push/pull fan-out, and what's the media-heavy twist versus a text feed?
points: Reuse the same hybrid fan-out: push photoIds into follower feeds for normal users, pull for high-follower accounts, merge at read.
The feed stores lightweight photoIds/metadata refs — NOT media — so fan-out amplification is cheap regardless of photo size.
The twist is hydration: after assembling photoIds, resolve each to its CDN variant URLs; the actual bytes are fetched by the client from the CDN.
Serve the right resolution per surface — thumbnails for grids, feed-size for scroll, full for detail — to control bandwidth.
Prefetch/lazy-load and progressive images to keep the media feed responsive on mobile.
questions.answer: Feed generation reuses the same push/pull hybrid: for normal users I fan out photoIds into follower timelines on write, for high-follower accounts I pull at read time, and merge the two. The crucial point is that the feed carries only lightweight photoId/metadata references, never media, so fan-out is just as cheap as a text feed regardless of the 2MB payloads. The media-heavy twist is hydration: once I have the photoIds I resolve each to its CDN variant URLs and the client fetches the bytes directly from the CDN, choosing thumbnail for grids, feed-size for scrolling, and full for detail. Serving the right resolution per surface, plus lazy-loading and progressive images, is what keeps a media feed responsive on mobile.

questions.prompt: Staff-level: cover durability, failure modes, and scale tradeoffs — what breaks, and how do you keep photos safe and delivery fast globally?
points: Durability: replicate blob storage across zones/regions (S3 multi-AZ + cross-region replication); metadata and blobs must not diverge — write blob first, then metadata, and reconcile orphans.
Failure: worker crash mid-processing → idempotent retry from the original; DB points to a not-yet-ready variant → serve original or placeholder until status=ready.
Orphan/consistency: garbage-collect blobs whose metadata write failed; treat metadata as source of truth for 'exists'.
Global delivery: geo-distributed CDN + regional S3 replicas so users fetch from a nearby edge; upload to nearest region.
Hot content: a viral photo is a CDN hot object — edge caching absorbs it; origin shielding prevents an origin stampede.
Cost tradeoff: tiered storage (hot recent photos on fast storage, cold archives to cheaper/Glacier), and cap generated variants to control storage multiplication.
questions.answer: Durability comes first: blobs are replicated multi-AZ and cross-region, and I order writes blob-first then metadata, treating metadata as the source of truth for existence and garbage-collecting orphaned blobs whose metadata write failed. Failure modes are handled by idempotent workers that reprocess from the durable original, and by serving the original or a placeholder whenever the DB references a variant that isn't ready yet. Globally, a geo-distributed CDN over regional S3 replicas lets users fetch from a nearby edge and upload to the nearest region; a viral photo becomes a hot CDN object that edge caching plus origin shielding absorb without stampeding S3. The main tradeoff is cost — I'd tier storage so hot recent photos sit on fast storage and cold archives move to cheaper/Glacier, and cap the number of generated variants since each one multiplies petabyte-scale storage.

diagrams.takeaway: Photo bytes flow directly to object storage while services and databases handle only metadata and coordination.

diagrams.takeaway: The upload becomes durable first; queued workers validate, scan, resize, and publish variants independently.

diagrams.title: Durable, globally delivered media
diagrams.takeaway: Cross-zone object replication protects originals, while lifecycle tiers and CDN caching control storage and egress cost.
